bio.en: Brian Halligan is co-founder and longtime CEO of HubSpot and now the in-house CEO coach at Sequoia, where he brings top CEOs together and coaches them one-on-one.
bio.zh: Brian Halligan 是 HubSpot 的联合创始人兼长期 CEO，现任红杉资本的驻场 CEO 教练，将顶尖 CEO 们聚集一堂并一对一带教。

summary.en: Brian argues that while starting a company has never been easier, scaling it into a durable, high-impact organization has never been harder, putting pressure on founders to decide faster. He shares the traits and “lock algorithm” he looks for in successful CEOs and what it's really like to carry that lonely responsibility. The conversation unpacks what it takes to be a successful CEO in today's faster-moving era.
summary.zh: Brian 认为，虽然创办公司从未如此容易，但把它扩展为持久、高影响力的组织却从未如此困难，这给创始人带来了更快决策的压力。他分享了成功 CEO 所需具备的特质和他寻找人才的“锁定算法”，以及承担这份孤独责任到底是什么滋味。对话拆解了在当今节奏更快的时代，成为成功 CEO 需要什么。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: The thing about being a founder/CEO is there is no one there to rescue you. Your parents aren't going to rescue you, your VC is not going to rescue you, that kind of hits you when you hit your first crisis.
turns.zh: 当创始人或者CEO最残酷的一点是，根本没人会来救你。父母不会来救你，投资人也不会来救你。这种感觉，往往要等你撞上第一次危机时，才会真正砸到你身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Starting a company has never been easier, scaling one into a durable high impact organization has never been harder.
turns.zh: 开一家公司，从来没有像今天这么容易；但要把它做成一个能持久、有巨大影响力的组织，也从来没有像今天这么难。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: The number of companies formed is going to much fewer over the next 10 years relative to the last 10 years, it's just going to be hard to stand out and really accelerate.
turns.zh: 未来十年成立的新公司数量，比起过去十年会少很多。因为要脱颖而出、真正实现加速增长，实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's most different about what it was like to be a CEO maybe 10, 20 years ago versus today?
turns.zh: 和十年、二十年前比，今天当CEO最大的不同到底是什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: There's a massive tax in optionality when you can move this fast and try a lot of things. It puts pressure on the CEOs to be faster and better decision makers.
turns.zh: 当你能行动得这么快、能尝试那么多事情时，保留过多选项是要付出巨大代价的。这就逼着CEO们必须更快、更好地做决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people in the world want to be founders, they want to be CEOs.
turns.zh: 这世上有很多人想当创始人，想当CEO。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I don't think anyone can do it. People talk about 9-9-6, it's way more than that. Founders are seven days a week, they're always on, [inaudible 00:00:44] Sunday nights, it's full contact.
turns.zh: 我觉得不是谁都能干这个的。大家老说996，其实远不止。创始人那是连轴转七天，时刻在线，周日晚上也得绷着，全程贴身肉搏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like there are specific profiles or traits to be successful?
turns.zh: 你觉不觉得，要当好CEO，得有某种特定的性格或者特质？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I look for four things, I call it my lock algorithm.
turns.zh: 我看四样东西，我管它叫LOCK法则。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure. I want to start with something that I've heard your board members, the way they described you, is someone with a perpetual state of constructive dissatisfaction. Do you think this is a core foundational trait of successful CEOs, successful leaders?
turns.zh: 是我的荣幸。我想先从一个我听你董事会成员描述你的词说起——他们说你处在一种'永远建设性的不满足'状态。你觉得这是成功CEO、成功领导者一个底层的核心特质吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: By the way, I like that description, when she did, a woman named Lorrie Norrington, who [inaudible 00:04:26] said that. I like it, I took it as kind of a compliment, and I liked it. So, I spend most of my time these days coaching very fast-growth CEOs. They all are kind of like that. They're all in kind of a state of perpetual dissatisfaction, but in a positive way. One of the things, by the way, I like about the current crop of CEOs, they don't really take stock of what they've done and feel it, they're always a little bit dissatisfied with where they are, and very focused on the end state. And I've been surprised at how humble this generation is of CEOs. And I think of my generation of CEOs as being, I don't know, humble wasn't the first word that would come out of your mouth when you describe my generation. But this generation I feel like is different, and I've been impressed with it.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我很喜欢这个描述。说这话的是一位叫Lorrie Norrington的女性。我很喜欢，把它当成了一种夸奖。我现在大部分时间都在辅导那些高速增长期的CEO，他们差不多都是这样——都处于一种永远不满足的状态，但是是正向的那种。话说回来，这一代CEO里有一点我很喜欢：他们不太去盘点自己已经做了什么、去沉浸在那份成就感里，而是永远对当下的位置有点不满足，死死盯着终点。而且这一代CEO的谦逊程度让我挺意外的。我们那一代CEO嘛，说实话，你形容我那代人的时候，脑子里蹦出来的第一个词肯定不是'谦逊'。但这一代真的不一样，让我挺刮目相看的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I have a bunch of questions along these lines, because one, you've been a CEO of an incredibly successful company for a long time, for about 20 years, before you moved on to this new chapter, now you work with a bunch of CEOs, you're Sequoia's in-house CEO coach, there's a few things that I've heard you do. One is you gather groups of CEOs, and what I've read is that you have kind of two tables. You have the kids table and the adults table. The kids table is CEOs that are companies that are about under 100 employees, the adult table is over 100 employees. So, let me ask you just, when you look at CEOs that move from the kids table to the adult table, other than just they scale and grow, what is it that these CEOs that graduate from kids to adults table do differently?
turns.zh: 好，顺着这个思路我有一堆问题。一来你做了很久的CEO，一家极其成功的公司干了快二十年，然后才开启新篇章；现在你又跟一堆CEO打交道，是红杉的驻场CEO教练。我听说你做了几件事，其中一件是你把CEO们聚成小组，而且我读到说你大概摆了两桌——'小孩桌'和'大人桌'。小孩桌是员工不到一百人的公司CEO，大人桌是一百人以上的。那我问你，当你看那些从小孩桌升级到大人桌的CEO，除了规模变大、人数变多，他们到底做错了什么、或者说做得不一样了？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: The adults are really focused on, all they really want to talk about is their exec team. Their direct reports, how do you build our exec team, that next level down, org design... You would be surprised how much they think about that. And on average, I would say the adults are spending half their time just recruiting and interviewing. It's pretty all consuming. And I remember that from that phase in HubSpot's growth. And it surprises people like, wow, my job is really just to interview and hire, I didn't know that was going to be the case. So, that is one that they are making that transition, and I would just say in general, people are very bad at this, and HubSpot was too. (00:06:57): I think CEOs and everyone dramatically overrates their ability to interview, and overrates their gut feeling, and underrates a really high quality blind reference. And I interviewed Dave, the CEO from MongoDB the other day, and he had an interesting [inaudible 00:07:22]. On average over his 10-year lifespan as a CEO of Mongo, there were two C-levels turned over per year. That's a lot of turnover at the top, and I didn't keep track of it like Dave, but I think HubSpot was kind of similar. And all of these startups are kind of similar too. And so, people are working on that, and struggling with it, is one thing in common with all of them.
turns.zh: 大人桌那些人真正在意的，翻来覆去就是他们的高管团队——他们的直接下属，怎么搭高管团队，下一层怎么搭，怎么设计组织结构……你想象不到他们为这个想了多少。平均来看，大人桌的CEO大概一半时间都在招人和面试，简直是全天候。HubSpot成长到那个阶段时我也是这样，而且这会让很多人吃惊：哇，合着我这工作就是面试和招人啊，我当初可没想到。所以这是他们正在经历的转变。总的来说，大家这方面都很差，HubSpot当年也一样。（00:06:57）我觉得CEO们，还有所有人，都严重高估了自己的面试能力，高估了自己的直觉，却低估了一份高质量'盲推'（blind reference）的价值。前几天我采访了MongoDB的CEO Dave，他有个挺有意思的观察。在他做Mongo CEO那十年里，平均每年有两个C-level高管走人。高层流动这么大，我没像Dave那样记，但我猜HubSpot也差不多，所有创业公司都差不多。所以大家都在跟这个较劲、被这个折磨，这是他们的一个共性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you do when you coach someone on that? When you're like, okay, you think you're amazing at interviewing, you think you know who's going to work out, what advice do you give them to help them develop that skill?
turns.zh: 你辅导这种事的时候具体怎么做？比如你说，你觉得你特会面试、觉得你能看准谁行谁不行，那你会给他们什么建议，帮他们练出这个本事？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think even me, I've been doing this for 150 years, I still think I overrate my ability to interview someone, and really know if they're a good fit. I give a couple pieces of advice. Parker Conrad has a good hack that I liked. Before he's got a C-level interview, CFO, chief product officer, whatever, he has some sign an NDA, and sends them the last board deck, or the board memo, or some important doc, and he schedules a half hour interview with them, and he just has a chat about the decks. And if they're just very complimentary, and it's so great, and you're doing this amazing thing, it's a major red flag to him because he wants someone that will challenge him and not a yes person. And I thought that was a pretty good hack to get inside someone's head and how they think and how they'll interact with you. (00:08:53): Getting on a whiteboard and working through a problem I think is always a good thing. I think the standard interview of walking through your background, I don't think is all that valuable. And I coach people to do blind references, find someone you know that work with them... VCs are good at this by the way. And I get a lot of these, and you can tell some of them are like, we've already decided we're checking the box, versus they're asking me hard questions about this person. And one of my favorite questions people ask is, would you enthusiastically rehire this person for that role? Which I think is a really good question. On a scale of one to 10, how likely is it that you'll try to rehire this person back from me down the road? (00:09:37): I think those types of questions are good, so not mailing an in on those blind references I think is really good. My other piece of advice, and no one listens to me on this, is hire slow and fire fast. People hire fast and fire slow. If I had to guess, Lenny, with 18 months after you hire a C-level exec, at least 50% of the time they're gone. High mortality rate on them, it's harder than people think.
turns.zh: 我觉得就算是我，都干了一百五十年了，我还是觉得我高估了自己的识人能力。我给几条建议。Parker Conrad有个我觉得挺妙的招。在面试一个C-level——不管是CFO还是CPO什么之前，他先让人家签个保密协议，然后把最近一次的董事会材料、或者董事会备忘录、或者什么重要文档发过去，再约半小时聊这些材料。他就光聊这些deck。如果对方只会一顿猛夸，'太棒了你们这活干得'，那对他来说就是个大红旗——他要的是能挑战他的人，不是应声虫。我觉得这招挺好，能钻进一个人的脑子，看他的思路和你们怎么互动。（00:08:53）在白板上一起推一个问题，我一直觉得是个好法子。至于那种走流程式的'讲讲你的履历'，我觉得价值不大。我还劝人做盲推——找你认识的、跟这个人共事过的人打听。VC这方面就挺在行。我接过不少这种电话，你能听出来有些人是已经内定、走个过场，有些是真的在认真问很难的问题。我最喜欢的一个问题是：如果让你重新招这个人干这个岗位，你会 enthusiastic 地再招一次吗？这问题就很到位。或者打分制：一到十分，你以后从我这把他挖回去的可能性有多大？（00:09:37）这类问题都很好，所以盲推千万别敷衍。我还有条建议，不过没人听我的——招人要慢，开人要快。大家都是招得快、开得慢。我猜啊Lenny，你招一个C-level进来，十八个月之内，至少一半概率人就没了。死亡率高得超出大家想象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, what you're saying here is there's only so much you can actually do to increase those odds.
turns.zh: 所以你说的意思是，你能真正去提高那个成功率的空间其实有限？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think you can, I think the blind references are key, I think doing real interactive, working on a project together is key. I'll tell you one of the things we learned at HubSpot about this. We would have a candidate come in, let's say a head of engineering, and we'd have eight people interview them. And our scale's one to four. And let's say four people were four out of four, and four people were two out of four. So, that's candidate A. And then the next candidate comes in, eight people interview them, and everyone's a three out of four. Almost every time we hired the three out of four, the person with the least amount of weaknesses. And we changed it, and we went with the spikier people, we went with people with weaknesses, we with people who would challenge stuff, and that has worked out quite well. (00:11:04): Our hit rate at HubSpot's improved. We also have shrunk the pool of people on that interview panel from eight to four. We just hired a head of product, and there were just four of us that interviewed them. I think that worked too. So, I think there's things you can do to get better at it, for sure.
turns.zh: 我觉得还是能的。盲推是关键，一起做个真刀真枪的实战项目也关键。跟你说个我们在HubSpot学到的。一个候选人来，比如工程负责人，我们让八个人面他，打分一到四。假设四个人给了满分四，四个人只给了二分，这是候选人A。下一个来，八个人面，每个人都是三分。结果我们几乎每次都招那个三分、也就是短板最少的。后来我们改了，专挑那些更'尖'的人，有缺点、但能挑战你的人，效果反而好得多。（00:11:04）HubSpot的命中率就上去了。而且我们把面试小组从八个人砍到了四个。我们刚招了一个产品负责人，就四个人面。我觉得这也对。所以，这方面肯定是有办法越做越好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. This is incredibly tactical and useful. On the references piece, the toughest part is getting people to be honest because there's very little upside to them to say negative things about people. Is there anything that you've learned to help get real honest answers from folks you call for references?
turns.zh: 好。这个非常实操、非常有用。说到推荐人这一块，最难的是让人家说真话，因为说人坏话对他们几乎没好处。你有没有学到什么招，能让那些你打去问推荐人的人，真的给出诚实的回答？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Well, I can just say I don't do this a lot anymore, but when people call me, I can tell if they've already decided, and when they're really just looking for... When they ask me for the strengths and weaknesses I'm like, oh, they've already decided. When they ask me something hard, like on a scale of one to 10, how likely you're to hire them again? Stuff like that, that kind of gets at the core. Or were they the top 1% of your employees? That's a good question. Oh, were they top 10? Oh. That type of question is pretty good. So, when I'm on the other side of it, I like when those types of questions come up. (00:12:16): I tell you the other mistake everyone makes, and all the CEOs we're making now, is you're hiring for that whatever, head of engineering, and you're blown away by the resume. Like you're 50 employees and you're hiring this person, who's been at Microsoft the last 10 years, and has a fancy title, and is a fancy division in Microsoft, and you hire them, there's just a massive impedance mismatch when you hire them on what their expectations are, and what your expectations are, in the extent that you get your shit together. It's just you don't. You definitely don't, if you're 50 or 500 employees. And they expect you to have your act together. So, that is another... Avoid the big company hire. We hired so many people from Salesforce, and Google, and Microsoft, like 100% attrition rate on all those folks.
turns.zh: 这个嘛，我现在自己做得少了，但别人打给我的时候，我能听出来他们是不是已经内定了，还是真在认真打听……当他们只问我这人的优缺点时，我心里就咯噔一下——哦，他们已经定了。当他们问很难的问题，比如'一到十分，你以后还会再招他吗'这种戳到本质的，我才觉得对路。或者'他算不算你手下前百分之一的员工'？这问题就好。哦，'前百分之十'？嗯……这类问题就挺好。所以反过来，当我是被问的那个，我也喜欢这类问题冒出来。（00:12:16）再告诉你一个所有人、包括现在这些CEO都在犯的错：你招一个什么工程负责人，被那份简历惊艳到了。你才五十个人，却招了个在微软干了十年、title光鲜、部门牛气的人，结果进来之后，你俩对'该有什么预期'的认知严重错配——你以为自己公司已经很正规了，其实根本没有。你真没有，不管你是五十人还是五百人。而人家预期你一切井井有条。所以这是另一个坑——别去大公司挖人。我们从Salesforce、Google、微软挖过太多人，结果百分之百都走光了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I've seen that a lot of companies is there's phases of like, okay, now it's the McKinsey, a cohort comes in, and we think that's going to be the answer, and then it's the Apple group, and then that didn't work out, then the Amazon group.
turns.zh: 我见过很多公司会有这种阶段——哦现在是麦肯锡帮，来一波人，觉得这下能解决问题了；然后是苹果帮；苹果帮不行了，又换成亚马逊帮。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: The McKinsey one never works. It never works. It never works. By definition, they would fail on my spectrum of... Most founders are like me, they are skeptical of dimensional wisdom, they're unhappy with the world works in some way, and so they're kind of far on that spectrum of rethinking dimensional wisdom. And almost by definition somebody who goes to work for McKinsey is very conservative in their outlook. And so, I think that almost always fails.
turns.zh: 麦肯锡那波永远不行，永远不行。说到底，按我的标准他们必败。大多创始人跟我一样，对本本上的所谓智慧是怀疑的，对这个世界某些运作方式是不爽的，所以他们在'重新思考既有智慧'这条光谱上是偏远的。而几乎凡是去麦肯锡的人，世界观都偏保守。所以我觉得那几乎必败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're on this s hiring thread, so let me keep following this conversation. I read somewhere that you recommend building your team like the 2004 Red Sox. What does this mean?
turns.zh: 我们还在聊招聘这条线，那我接着问。我好像在哪读到过，你建议像组建2004年的红袜队那样搭团队。这是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Well, I'm a big sports fan, a big Boston Red... And the Boston Red Sox hadn't won, Lenny, a World Series in 86 years, since they traded Babe Ruth.
turns.zh: 我是个超级体育迷，铁杆波士顿红袜粉……红袜队在交易掉贝比·鲁斯之后，整整八十六年没拿过世界大赛冠军。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember that.
turns.zh: 这个我记得。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: And they finally broke, and they finally won it in 2004. And the way they won it was they had a team of a bunch homegrown, really high quality, inexpensive talent that they drafted and came through the farm system. And then they got a few free agents, like David Ortiz, that a lot of people have heard of, that they paid a fair amount of money to. Peter Martinez and Curt Schilling were kind of the canonical older been there, done that, bigger company folks. And they mixed really nicely, the culture really worked. And I think that's the key. I think people underrate their homegrown talent, almost across the board they underrate it. And I think you want that mix. You don't want to hire a whole bunch of been there, done that, and you don't want to hire [inaudible 00:14:57].
turns.zh: 后来他们终于破了咒，2004年拿下了。他们能赢，靠的是一群自家培养、质量极高、还便宜的新秀——都是自己选秀、从农场系统里磨出来的。然后他们又弄了几个自由球员，比如大家都听过的David Ortiz，花了一大笔钱。Pedro Martinez和Curt Schilling算是那种典型的'老江湖'——去过大公司、什么都见过了的老将。这几拨人混在一起特别顺，文化也搭。我觉得关键就在这。大家普遍低估了自己培养的人，几乎全都低估。而你要的是这种混合。你既不想全招'老江湖'，也不想全招……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine this is public, but you're now part owner of the Red Sox, is that right?
turns.zh: 我猜这是公开的，你现在还是红袜队的股东之一，对吧？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I am a part owner of the Red Sox, yes.
turns.zh: 对，我是红袜队的股东之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I have questions for you along those lines.
turns.zh: 好，顺着这个我有几个问题。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's amazing advice. Kind of what I'm taking away here is people see all these fancy logos, amazing person, VP, this, that at Salesforce, Amazon, Google, whatever, and what you're saying here is don't underestimate the power of someone internal, rising to the occasion.
turns.zh: 好，这建议太赞了。我从中得到的启发是：大家看到那些闪闪发光的logo，什么Salesforce、亚马逊、Google的VP、牛人，但你在这里说的是——别低估内部人临危受命的爆发力。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah. If you look at HubSpot, half the management team are folks who had been there for approximately 150 years, which I like. And same with, you look at Apple, a lot of those people are homegrown.
turns.zh: 对。你看HubSpot，管理团队里有一半是在那待了差不多一百五十年的人，我很喜欢这点。苹果也一样，很多人都是自己长出来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, is there any tips here for doing this well, is it just give people a chance?
turns.zh: 那要搞好这件事有什么窍门吗？就是给机会就行？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I tend to give people a chance. It's like, if you're interviewing someone that's homegrown, and they're VP for that C-level job, versus hiring someone from the outside. I hire someone from the outside, they're very good at interviewing, from a big company, they look fancy, they're shiny, you haven't seen their warts, hard to figure out their warts unless you're very good at line referencing, and so you tend to overrate them and underrate your homegrown. So, if it's pretty close, I think you give your homegrown a shot at it. (00:16:03): What's interesting to me, Lenny, is Brian Chesky sort of rethought a lot of this stuff, and he's like everyone's over-rotating to the homegrown to the experienced talent and management teams and delegation, I think he's mostly right about that. People haven't really followed that. People are, they're hiring people from the outside quite a bit. That's kind of the standard part of the playbook that all of them are following now. It's a little different, it's actually quite different than what Brian [inaudible 00:16:32].
turns.zh: 我倾向于给人机会。比如，你面一个内部成长起来的人，他已经是那个C-level岗位的VP了，对比从外面招一个。外面招来的，面试特别溜，大公司出来的，光鲜，但你看不到他的毛病——除非你盲推做得极好，否则很难看穿，所以你容易高估他、低估自己人。所以要是两头差不多，我倾向给自家人一个机会。（00:16:03）有意思的是Lenny，Brian Chesky其实把这套重新想了一遍，他觉得大家都在过度往'自己人'和'有经验的高管团队加授权'那头偏，我觉得他大体是对的，但大家并没真跟上。现在大家还是在相当频繁地从外面招人，那是所有人都在用的标准打法。其实跟Brian想的有点不一样，差得还挺多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to the conversation around CEOs, a lot of people listening to this podcast, just a lot of people in the world want to be founders, they want to be CEOs. At the same time, you look at Elon, you look at Jensen, you look at Steve Jobs, you look at you, a lot of people are like, I can't. I'm not this person, I'm not going to be as good as them. There's no world where I'm this good. Do you feel like there are specific profiles or just traits that you have to be born with to be a successful CEO, or do you think it's earnable, anybody can be successful if they really work hard?
turns.zh: 回到CEO这个话题。很多听这播客的人，就是这世上很多想当创始人、想当CEO的人。但同时你看Elon、看Jensen、看Steve Jobs、看你自己，很多人会想：我不行，我不是那种人，我达不到他们那个高度，根本没可能那么强。你觉得当好CEO是得有某种特定的性格、甚至是天生的特质，还是说靠努力就能练出来，谁拼命干都能成功？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Go ahead and meet all these CEOs coming in, and I have a little algorithm in my head, and I look for four things. I call it my LOCK algorithm. L is for lovable, and Steve Jobs you would say is kind of rough and maybe not lovable, but he would inspire followership. You would want to follow him. And so, could I envision a 28-year-old me, graduating from business school, going to work for this person? Would I crawl across broken glass? That's question one. Two is just obsession. Are they deeply obsessed with this problem? I'm a little negative on people who came up with this problem to solve six months ago and started a company, I like people with deep founder market fit, who've been thinking about it for a long time, and have evidence in their lives of going deep down, obsessively down a rabbit hole because that's kind of what it takes to be a founder/CEO. (00:18:02): The C is something I wouldn't have thought of, but this is a Sequoia thing, like chip on the shoulder. Pretty much all of them have a boulder on their shoulder, and I have a bit of a chip on my shoulder too. And the K is just for deeply knowledgeable about the domain. And so, I look for that. If I were to stick an S on it, I would say student. I look at Winston Weinberg from Harvey, or James from Profound, or Gabe from Rogo, some of these new very fast growing companies, they're students of the game. They're not just learn it alls, they're deep, deep, deep students of the game. And they're like LLMs, they're constantly, constantly learning, and it's not just learning stuff for me and their peers, but they go way back in time, and have a lot of history on stuff. So, those are some of the, kind of my little criteria I use when I'm evaluating CEOs. What do you look for, by the way, you've interviewed a ton of folks like me, what do you think is in common?
turns.zh: 你去见那些新来的CEO，我脑子里有个小算法，专门看四样东西，我管它叫LOCK法则。L是lovable（讨人喜欢）。你说Steve Jobs有点糙、可能不算lovable，但他能激发人追随，你愿意跟着他。所以我会问自己：一个28岁的我，商学院刚毕业，愿不愿意去给这人打工？愿不愿意为他爬过碎玻璃？这是第一个问题。第二个是obsession（痴迷）。他们是不是对这个问题死磕到底？我对那种'半年前才想到这个问题、然后开了个公司'的人是有点负面看法的，我喜欢那种跟这个问题有深度'创始人-市场契合'的人——想了很久，生活里就有证据显示他一头扎进兔子洞、 obsessive 地钻研，因为要当创始人兼CEO基本就靠这个。（00:18:02）C是我以前没想到的，但这是红杉的一个说法，叫chip on the shoulder（不服气、憋着一股劲）。他们几乎人人肩上都扛着块大石头，我肩上也有点。K就是deeply knowledgeable，对自己这个领域极懂。所以我看这些。要是再塞个S上去，我会说student——学生。你看Harvey的Winston Weinberg、Profound的James、Rogo的Gabe，这些飞快成长的新公司，他们都是这门游戏的学生。不是单纯爱学习，是 deep deep deep 的学生。他们像LLM一样，不停地学，而且不只是为自己和同辈学，还往回追溯很远，对很多事有历史纵深。这些就是我评估CEO时用的几条标准。对了，你呢？你采访过这么多像我这种人，你觉得共性是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of what successful founders? Oh my god. I wish I had the... My succinct answer, I would go to Lennybot.com, and be like, what is the common pattern across these folks? One that you didn't mention that I think is interesting, I did some research on this recently, with Terence Rohan, one is just extremely ambitious. Just trying to do something really wild that most people are like, that's crazy. You're not going to get a subscription service for all music in the world, that's just... What are you doing? [inaudible 00:19:38]-
turns.zh: 成功创始人的共性？天哪。我要是能一句话答上来就好了……我的简版答案是，我会去Lennybot.com问：这些人里共同的模式是什么？有一点你没提到、但我觉得特别有意思——我最近和Terence Rohan做了点研究——就是极度有野心。就是想干那种特别野的事，野到大多数人都觉得'你疯了吧'。你不可能做出一个覆盖全世界所有音乐的订阅服务，你这是在搞什么？……

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: [inaudible 00:19:40]. Is it learnable? I notice some of, a lot of the CEOs struggling with a couple of things. Like let's say you're Winston, you're late 20s, you've never managed a team, you're probably never even captain of a sports team before, and in order to scale, you have to give people feedback constantly. It's very unnatural. It's like, I'm going to give this VP I hired a bunch of feedback, positive and negative. And if you don't get good at that, you really pay the price later. That's something I think they have to learn. They all have to learn to get a good bullshit detector. They're constantly being spun, everyone's trying to sell to them, the org is always trying to sell to them. So, that's sort of something they have to develop over time. (00:20:29): They have to all get good at the inspiration thing over time. Like, you're Winston, you've never had to inspire anyone in your entire life. You went to school, and you're a lawyer for a few years, and you started this thing... Inspiration wasn't your thing. So, there's certain things you have to learn on that startup to scale up path, and the best ones learn it very fast.
turns.zh: （听不清00:19:40）这个能学吗？我注意到有些、其实很多CEO在几件事上挣扎。比如你是Winston，二十来岁，从没管过团队，可能连运动队队长都没当过，但要规模化，你就得不停地给人反馈，正面负面都得给。这非常反本能。就像，我要给我招来的这个VP一大堆反馈。你要是学不会这个，后面代价很大。这是我觉得他们必须学的。他们所有人都要练出可靠的' bullshit 探测器'——他们无时无刻不在被人忽悠，人人都想卖东西给他们，组织内部也总在向他们推销。所以这是得慢慢长出来的。（00:20:29）他们还都得慢慢学会'激励'这件事。比如你是Winston，这辈子从没激励过任何人。你上过学，当过几年律师，然后开了这摊事……激励不是你的强项。所以在'从起步到规模化'这条路上，有些东西必须学，学得最快的才是最厉害的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is extremely interesting and useful. So, LOCK, with an S at the end, just to kind of mirror back what you're sharing. And when you were saying you evaluate CEOs, is this for investing as a-
turns.zh: 这个极其有意思、极有用。所以LOCK，末尾加个S，我把你刚说的镜像回来一下。你说评估CEO是在投资时……

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. Yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so when you're helping Sequoia decide should we invest in this company, what you look for is, LOCK... I like the S, I'm going to include it there. So, are they lovable? Are they inspiring? O, are they obsessed with this problem they're going after? Do they have a chip on their shoulder? Are they extremely knowledgeable about the problem they're going after? And it sounds like not just the problem but just the studying company's business strategy, things like that. And then, S was a student. I guess that's what S is, student is studying, being a founder, being a CEO. Okay. So, I guess going back just to the question, do you think, just to put it very simply, do you think CEOs are born, or do you think they're made? Can anyone turn into an amazing CEO?
turns.zh: 好，所以当你帮红杉判断该不该投这家公司时，你看的就是LOCK……我喜欢那个S，我把它加进去。那他们是lovable吗？能激发人吗？O，他们是不是对要解决的问题痴迷？他们是不是憋着一股劲？他们对自己要解决的问题是不是极懂？而且听起来不只是问题本身，还包括研究公司的商业战略之类的。然后S是学生。我猜S就是这个——学生，研究、当创始人、当CEO。好。那回到开头那个问题，说得简单点，你觉得CEO是天生的，还是练出来的？谁都能变成厉害的CEO吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I don't think anyone can do it, I don't think it's just anyone. I will say, I've noticed... So, another little rubric I have, and I don't see a lot of these, but Brett Taylor's one, there's a few out there that are in Sequoia's portfolio. I call them back to the baseball thing, a five tool player. In baseball when you rank a player it's, can they hit? Can they hit with power? Can they run? Can they catch a ball? Can they throw the ball? And they rate them one to 10 at each. And it's very rare that you have a five tool player, extremely rare. And the thing that's kind of new now, are there are five tools CEOs, like Brett Taylor's one. (00:22:24): You can code, you have taste, you have vision, you can sell the product, you can convince employees. This kind super CEO. And there's a bunch of them now. And I don't know, I didn't see a lot of those. That certainly wasn't Steve Jobs, he wasn't programming. It wasn't Jeff Bezos. I think there's kind of a new breed that's quite impressive.
turns.zh: 我觉得不是谁都能干，不是随便谁都行。不过我注意到……我还有另一个小标尺，这种人不多见，但Brett Taylor算一个，红杉 portfolio 里还有几个。我借棒球那个说法，叫'五工具球员'。棒球评一个球员，是看他能不能打、能不能长打、能不能跑、能不能接、能不能传，每项打一到十分。五项全强的极其罕见。现在新鲜的是，出现了'五项全能CEO'，比如Brett Taylor就是。（00:22:24）你能写代码、有品位、有vision、能把产品卖出去、能说服员工。这种超级CEO。现在有一批了。说实话我以前少见，Steve Jobs肯定不算，他不会编程；Jeff Bezos也不算。我觉得出现了一类挺吓人的新物种。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These folks you mentioned were this good before AI became a thing, I imagine AI helps more CEOs fill the gaps that they have.
turns.zh: 你提的这些人，在AI出现之前就已经这么强了。我猜AI能帮更多CEO补上他们的短板。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think AI is, it's hard to fill the gap of this guy's a developer, he's genius level, obsessive, but can he sell? Can he convince an investor to give him a lot of money and a high valuation? Can he convince brilliant employees to leave OpenAI and join him? Can he convince some big skeptical Fortune 500 enterprise to buy his product? Being able to do that, and have taste, and be able to code really well at next levels, I think is rare. I actually think it might be the other way though, where mere mortals like me, who can kind of code, all of a sudden we're going to be able to build stuff. I think it kind of goes the other way.
turns.zh: 我觉得AI很难补上这种人的短板——他是开发、是天才级、是痴迷型，但他会不会卖？能不能说服投资人给他大笔钱、高估值？能不能说服牛人离开OpenAI来跟他？能不能说服某个将信将疑的财富500强企业买他的产品？能搞定这些、有品位、还能写到下一个层次的代码，我觉得这种人 rare。不过我反而觉得可能是反过来的——像我这种凡人，勉强会点代码，突然之间我们也能搞出东西了。我觉得方向可能是反的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this list you shared of things that you find CEOs most have to learn. BS detection, inspiring people, giving hard feedback. Maybe the one thing that most often people that become CEOs/founders have to work on, is there a most common thread of, here's the thing you probably need to work on most?
turns.zh: 你列的这些CEO大多得学的东西我特别喜欢：识破忽悠、激励人、给难听的反馈。如果说成为CEO或创始人最普遍要补的课，有没有一条最常见的主线——就是最该下功夫的那件事？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: It's that feedback thing. All of the CEOs are building their teams, and so many are like, I have a co-founder that runs product and engineering, but I need that co-founder to step aside and be the CTO, and the thinker, and the labs person, and I need to hire somebody who can actually run the engineering machine. So many of the CEOs are going through that right now. That's a tricky transition. So many of the CEOs are layering folks, like you hired that early head of sales, he hired 10 people, but just can't quite figure out the sales profile, can't quite unpack the sales process, can't quite forecast accurately. We need to layer the person. (00:24:46): Those types of conversations are very tricky and quite unnatural for homo sapiens to have if you're 25 and you've never done anything like that before. So, I see the best ones getting really good at that and studying it, and it's super uncomfortable, but they have to suck it up and get good at it.
turns.zh: 是反馈那件事。所有CEO都在搭团队，很多人会说：我有个联合创始人管产品和工程，但我需要让他退下来当CTO、当那个思考者、当labs的人，我得另招一个真能运转工程机器的人。现在很多CEO都在经历这个，这是个棘手的转变。还有很多人是在'叠人'——你招了那个早期销售负责人，他招了十个人，但就是搞不清销售画像、拆不开销售流程、预测也不准。我们得在头上叠一个人。（00:24:46）这类对话非常棘手，对二十来岁、从没干过这种事的人来说，简直反人类。所以我看到最厉害的那些人，逼着自己把这个练熟、去研究它，过程超级不舒服，但他们得咬牙扛过去、把它学会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you find most helps them build these skills, get better at this? Is there some tidbits of advice you give them? Is it something that they study to improve?
turns.zh: 你觉得什么最能帮他们练出这些本事？你给他们什么小建议？是靠学吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think misery loves company on this. So, what I do, the table is 15 CEOs of companies under 100 employees and the adults' table are CEOs of companies over 100 employees, about 15 of them. They talk about this with each other, it's kind of a safe space, and I can weigh in, but it's actually much more effective when their peers weigh in. I think misery really does like company on stuff like this. They learn from each other.
turns.zh: 我觉得这里是'难友抱团'。所以我的做法是：小孩桌是十五个不到一百人公司的CEO，大人桌是一百人以上的CEO，也是大概十五个。他们互相聊这些，算个安全屋，我也能插嘴，但其实同行之间的反馈有效得多。这种事上，难友真的喜欢聚在一起。他们互相学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, essentially it's find peers to talk to and share and be vulnerable and open.
turns.zh: 所以本质上就是：找同行去聊、去分享、去示弱、去敞开。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: [inaudible 00:25:45]. And the reason I break it out is the problems with the kids' table are very different than the problems of the adult table. And they all rhyme, they rhyme a lot.
turns.zh: （听不清00:25:45）我之所以把它分开，是因为小孩桌的问题和大人桌的问题很不一样。但它们都'押韵'，押得很厉害。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you teach a course at MIT around scaling startups, and it's specifically around scaling, not startups, not starting the company. And you have this quote in your syllabus, "Starting a company has never been easier, scaling one into a durable high impact organization has never been harder." Why is that the case?
turns.zh: 你在MIT开一门关于规模化创业公司的课，而且专门讲规模化，不是起步、不是开公司。你教学大纲里有句话：'开公司从未如此容易，把它做成一个持久、有巨大影响力的组织从未如此之难。'为什么会这样？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Has it ever been easier to start a company? It's so easy-
turns.zh: 开公司什么时候比现在更容易过？太容易了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's absolutely true.
turns.zh: 那绝对是真的。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: And the flip side of that is, how many companies... The number of companies formed is going to mushroom over the next 10 years relative to the last 10 years, and the last 10 years compared to the previous 10 years is mushroomed. I just think in my life, I'm old, and when I was a kid I'd walked into CVS corner drug store and I wanted to buy a toothbrush, there are four or five there, you pick one. And in the 90s or 2000s you go to Amazon, there are four or 5,000 toothbrushes. Four or 5,000 companies bringing us toothbrushes. It got much, much easier to make stuff. (00:26:58): And even technology. AWS just made it easier to start a software company. So, it's like a huge jump, back then when we started HubSpot in 2006, but now it's going to be an even bigger jump. So, it's easier to start. Now, there's so much noise and competition, it's just going to be hard to stand out and really accelerate and scale. So, that's why I say it's never been easier to start, there's never been more competition, it's never been harder to scale.
turns.zh: 反过来，多少公司……未来十年成立的新公司数量，会比过去十年多得多，而过去十年比再前十年又已经多了一大截。我就想啊，我老了，小时候走进CVS街角药店想买把牙刷，货架上就四五把，挑一把。到了九零、零零年代你去亚马逊，有四五千把牙刷。四五千家公司给你供牙刷。做东西变得容易太多了。（00:26:58）技术也是。AWS就让开软件公司容易了。所以对比我们2006年刚开HubSpot时，那是巨大一跳，而现在会是更大的一跳。所以起步更容易。但现在噪音和竞争这么多，要脱颖而出、真的加速、规模化，太难了。所以我才说：起步从未如此容易，竞争从未如此之多，规模化从未如此之难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a big part of this is distribution, essentially, breaking through the noise is what I'm hearing?
turns.zh: 而这里大头就是'分发'，说白了就是突破噪音，对吧？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah. And it's hard to learn that. You didn't grow up doing distribution, you don't know. So, they're all learning it, and the ones that learn fast... It's like a learning game, the faster you learn, the better you do.
turns.zh: 对。而且这个很难学。你不是长着做分发的能力长大的，你不懂。所以他们都在学，学得快的……这是个学习游戏，学得越快越好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, I saw you tweet this recently, where people talk about which jobs AI is going to replace, and you said that sales is maybe the last job AI will replace. Why do you think that's the case?
turns.zh: 顺着这个，我看到你最近发了条推文，大家都在聊AI会取代哪些工作，你说销售可能是AI最后才会取代的工作。为什么这么看？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Well, if you look inside a typical enterprise, where's AI really working? Let's say inside of HubSpot. Software development is working incredibly well. Customer support, incredibly well. Legal starting to work incredibly well. But there really aren't apps in the rest of the org that have really changed things a lot. And in the go-to-market side has been kind of slow, really just support. There isn't a canonical marketing, or sales, or... Maybe the BDR is the first one. But I think ye old enterprise sales, where there's actual trust built up between two carbon-based life forms, I think will be very, very, very late to go in the white collar world. (00:28:42): I think a lot about the go-to-market. I think the go-to-market is going to get turned on its head. When we started HubSpot, if I think of the way the funnel worked, you want to get found in Google, someone clicks on a blue link, they land on your website, they go down the rabbit hole, they clicked on contact sales, they wait until that sales rep's ready, go down that rabbit hole, and I think it's going to get turned on its head, where people are evaluating a product, they start in Gemini or they start in Anthropic, or they start in ChatGPT, (00:29:12): And for example, ChatGPT knows everything on your website, everything beyond that, knows all your competitors. So, they will stay in there and do lots more research, and be incredibly well-educated. So, your website's a lot less important. And then they go to your site, I think sites will change where you're going to have a really high quality avatar that knows everything about your products, knows everything about your company, and your pricing, and packaging, and you can have a high quality conversation with that person. That person that will get stored in your CRM, and will get scored. (00:29:46): Is this is good quality conversation? And then the sales rep will follow up. But that sales rep will bring an avatar with them on every sales call. You won't have to wait for their SC, they'll have their own SC that's all knowing, that will follow them through the process. So, go-to-market hasn't changed much yet, but I think over time it's going to change a lot.
turns.zh: 你看一家典型大企业里，AI到底在哪真起作用？比如HubSpot内部。软件开发跑得极好，客服极好，法务也开始极好。但组织其他部门，真没几个应用带来大变化，go-to-market（推向市场）这块一直慢，基本就客服。还没有一个标杆性的营销、或销售、或……也许BDR（业务开发代表）是第一个。但我觉得那种老派的企业销售——两个碳基生物之间真正建立起信任的那种——在白领世界里会非常非常非常晚才被替代。（00:28:42）我很爱想go-to-market这件事。它会被彻底掀翻。我们刚开HubSpot时，漏斗是这样工作的：你在Google被搜到，有人点那个蓝链接，落到你网站，钻进兔子洞，点'联系销售'，等销售准备好，再走一遍兔子洞。我觉得这会整个翻过来——人们评估一个产品，是从Gemini、从Anthropic、从ChatGPT开始的。（00:29:12）比如ChatGPT知道你网站上的每一句话、知道你网站之外的所有东西、知道你所有竞争对手。所以他们会待在那里面做大量研究，变得极其懂行。于是你的网站就没那么重要了。然后他们去你网站，我觉得网站会变——你会有一个极懂行的虚拟形象，懂你所有产品、所有公司、所有定价和打包方式，你能跟它好好聊一场。这个人的信息会存进你的CRM，被打分。（00:29:46）'这是一场高质量的对话吗？'然后销售再去跟进。但那个销售每次打电话，都会带一个虚拟形象一起上。你不会……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This avatar, just so I understand. So, this is the buyer has their own little agent that comes with them? Or on HubSpot you have this avatar that walks you through the sales process?
turns.zh: 这个虚拟形象，我理解一下——是说买家自己带个小agent来？还是说在HubSpot这边，你有个虚拟形象带你走销售流程？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think both. I think me as a knowledge worker, what I really want as a homo sapien is I have a Delphi clone that I really like.
turns.zh: 我觉得两者都是。作为一个知识工作者，我这个碳基人真正想要的，是一个我特别喜欢的Delphi克隆体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same.
turns.zh: 我也是。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: It's actually quite good.
turns.zh: 其实还挺好用的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. [inaudible 00:30:28].

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do people find yours?
turns.zh: 人们去哪找你的那个？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: They find it on my footer, they can find it on Delphi-
turns.zh: 在页脚能找到，在Delphi上也能找到——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. We'll link to it.
turns.zh: 好，我们会放链接。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah. And what I want is connect that thing to my email, into my Granola, into my plot, and it knows everything about me. And then, when I go to a meeting, Lenny, I want to invite that thing to my meeting. So, it's sitting there in the Zoom meeting, it's not just taking notes like Granola, it's a participant. So, if I forgot something, I ask it a question, if somebody else forgot... I think every knowledge worker will have one of these in 3, 4, 5 years. But mine was more on the go-to-market side, where I think every website will change and there'll be an all-knowing avatar on that homepage. And if it's a considered purchase, I think it gets handed off to a sales rep, and that sales rep has a conversation, but when that sales rep's on Zoom, they have their SE avatar that's kind of all-knowing. And so, I think this stuff all changes a lot in the next few years, but it hasn't really unlocked yet.
turns.zh: 对。而我想要的是，把这个东西连到我的邮箱、连到我的Granola、连到我的plot，它对我的一切了如指掌。然后Lenny，我去开会时，想把这个东西也邀请进会议。它就坐在Zoom里，不只是像Granola那样记笔记，它是个参与者。我要是忘了什么，问它；别人忘了，也问它。我觉得三五年之内，每个知识工作者都会有一个这种东西。但我的更偏go-to-market那侧——我觉得每个网站都会变，首页上会有一个全知的虚拟形象。如果是需要慎重考虑的大宗购买，我会把它交给一个销售，那个销售去聊，但他在Zoom上时，身边带着一个全知的SE虚拟形象。所以我觉得接下来几年这些都会大变，只是还没真正解锁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are we going to be doing in this world, these two bots chatting with each other?
turns.zh: 那在这个世界里我们干啥？俩bot互相聊？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: It's going to be great, Lenny. You and I are going to be sitting on-
turns.zh: 会特别爽的Lenny。你我就坐在——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're into podcasts.
turns.zh: 我们在播客里。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: We're in Turks and Caicos, relaxing, on a month-long vacation, sending our avatars to all the meetings.
turns.zh: 我们在 Turks and Caicos，瘫着，放一个月假，派我们的虚拟形象去开所有会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go buy me some HubSpot seats please. I think this is why ClawdBot was so popular. I think this is essentially what they're building, is this idea. Which is now called Moltbot, which might be changing again. It's just this personal agent that can go do stuff for you.
turns.zh: 去给我买几个HubSpot席位哈。我觉得ClawdBot为什么那么火，就是因为这个——他们其实在做的就是这个想法，现在叫Moltbot，可能又要改名字了。就是这种能替你跑腿办事的个人agent。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you're talking about the future of go-to-market is this world where there's these little bots and agents that are doing things for you on both sides. When you look at companies today that you work with, that are doing well, that are especially AI-driven companies, what are they doing differently in terms of go-to-market that is working really well?
turns.zh: 所以你说go-to-market的未来，就是两边都有这种小bot、小agent替你干活的世界。那你看现在你辅导的那些公司、那些做得好的、尤其是AI驱动的公司，他们在go-to-market上到底做了什么不一样的事，而且真管用？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Honestly, the only thing that's different today, it's exactly the same as it's been for 100 years, except they call their SCs or their system consultants for deployed engineers. The rest of it is the same. I thought it would be totally different in AI, and working with all these companies, they're hiring all the same folks, running the same enterprise sales processes. So, it hasn't changed that much, at least on the enterprise side. Actually, I spent the first 10 years of my career at a company called PTC, which is like an enterprise sales machine. Enterprise sales hasn't changed that much since the 1990s.
turns.zh: 老实说，今天唯一不一样的，跟一百年前完全一样，只是他们把SC（解决方案顾问）或者现场部署工程师换了个名。其余都一样。我本来以为AI会让它彻底不同，但跟这么多公司打交道下来，他们招的还是同一拨人，跑的还是同一套企业销售流程。所以至少在企服侧，没怎么变。其实我职业生涯头十年在一家叫PTC的公司，那就是个企业销售机器。企业销售自九十年代起就没怎么变过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, forward deployed engineer, a very hot term, the idea there is they come work with the customer and help them implement this thing. And that's come up a lot on this podcast just with AI tools, rarely are they just plug and play, you can't just set up some agent that figures everything out. Takes a lot of onboarding and integration. Is it actually a different thing at all versus sales engineering in the past, things like that, or-
turns.zh: 那'现场部署工程师'这个很火的词，核心是说他们去跟客户一起干、帮客户把东西落地。这档播客聊AI工具时经常冒出来——很少有什么是即插即用的，你不可能就摆个agent让它自己搞定一切，要大量 onboarding 和集成。那它跟过去的销售工程到底有没有真的不同？还是——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think it's a solutions consultant sales engineer.
turns.zh: 我觉得就是解决方案顾问、销售工程师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: They're technical, and they help you implement it, they connect all your systems, they customize it. It's different. You're training it in a different way, but... Well, anyway, I think the term is fine. I'm sort of being light on it because, boy, it looks similar except that role has a different name to it.
turns.zh: 他们是技术型的，帮你落地、把你的系统全接上、帮你定制。是有不同，你训练它的方式不一样，但是吧……总之这个词没问题。我之所以说得轻巧，是因为兄弟，除了名字换了，看着太像了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, if anything, the device I'm hearing here is just lean into this, continue to lean into this idea of having your employees help the customer on board, be successful, integrate all that stuff.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以如果说有什么可操作的，就是你放心大胆地沿着这个思路走——继续让你们的员工帮客户做onboard、帮客户成功、做集成这些事。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I think the thing that will change first is the top of the funnel around getting found inside Google, you got to get found in these...
turns.zh: 我觉得最先变的，是漏斗顶端那块'在Google被搜到'——你必须在这些……里被找到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, AEO.
turns.zh: 对，AEO（答案引擎优化）。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah, that's going to be really important. And the way you build your website is very different for that to optimize for it. And then, I think your homepage is totally different. I think you land on an avatar and have a conversation with them, versus you're going through all the pages on your site. I think the top of the funnel is about changed a lot.
turns.zh: 对，这个会极其重要。而你建网站的方式也得为这个大改。然后我觉得你的首页会彻底不同——你落到一个虚拟形象上，跟它聊，而不是翻你网站所有页面。我觉得漏斗顶端会变很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Has anyone doing this well yet, this idea of this avatar or is this just kind of in the future-
turns.zh: 现在有人把这个做好的吗？这种虚拟形象的想法，还是说这只是在未来——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: There's a few startup programs. HubSpot does it, we built one, it's working.
turns.zh: 有几个创业项目在做。HubSpot就做了，我们做了一个，管用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh. Okay. Okay. Let me ask one more question around CEO stuff, and then I want to move on to Halliganisms.
turns.zh: 哦。好，好。那我再问一个关于CEO的问题，然后我想进'Halliganisms'（霍尔甘语录）环节。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How is just being a CEO different than it was? So, you've been doing this for 20-ish years, what's most different about what it was like to be a CEO maybe 10, 20 years ago versus today?
turns.zh: 当CEO到底哪里不一样了？你干这行二十年左右，跟十年、二十年前比，当CEO最大的不同是什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: One of my... It was actually Winston from Harvey, said this a year ago, and I was like, that's bullshit, but I actually think he was right. He, he's like, "You can just do a lot more." You've got AI agents doing stuff, everyone's more productive, the software developers are more productive. Something that used to take you a year takes two months now. And so, the amount of projects and the amount of stuff you can do is much, much more, I think he's right. I think that's a little dangerous. Let's say you found your beachhead market, and that beachhead market is really good, and it's very deep, there's a lot of work to do, I think what's dangerous for companies is they hop to that second act too quickly, and they lose focus on that first act. (00:35:21): And this isn't a completely perfect analogy, but you think of OpenAI and ChatGPT, and its consumer app is doing incredible, and they're doing lots and lots and lots and lots of other things, and then Gemini comes out and they've kind of focused back on the core. I think there's a lot of competition, everything is moving fast. I do think people get more done, and I think that impacts everything. The planning cycles used to be a year, I think the planning cycles now are three months long. Yeah, that's a big change. I think it puts pressure on the CEOs to be faster and better decision makers. (00:36:01): I just think of times in HubSpot when things slowed down and there was churn, it was usually my fault. It was because there were some hard one-way door type decisions on my desk, and maybe every year I would sit down and I'd open that one-way door or close it, and it just freed everyone up and we just started moving so much faster. I think people need to be making those decisions and walking through those doors much more quickly than they used to. I think that's new and different. I was someone who always valued optionality, I think there's a massive tax in optionality when you can move this fast and try a lot of things. So, I do think the job's changing a lot.
turns.zh: 我有个……其实是Harvey的Winston一年前说的，我当时觉得'扯淡'，但其实他是对的。他说：'你能干的事多太多了。'你有AI agent在跑，大家都更高效，开发也更高效。以前要一年的事现在两个月就搞定。所以你能做的项目、能搞的事，多太多了，我觉得他是对的。但我觉得这有点危险。比如你找到了自己的滩头市场，而且那个市场特别好、特别深，活很多，危险的是公司太早跳去第二幕，把第一幕的专注丢了。（00:35:21）这不算完全贴切的类比，但你想OpenAI和ChatGPT，它的消费端app牛得不行，同时它又在搞无数别的事，然后Gemini出来，它又把重心拉回核心。我觉得竞争很激烈，一切都在飞快动。我确实觉得人们能干成更多，而这影响了一切。计划周期以前是一年，现在我觉得是三个月。对，这是个大变化。它逼着CEO必须更快、更好地决策。（00:36:01）我就想起HubSpot几次放慢、出现人员流失的时候，通常都是我的锅。因为有些难的一锤定音的'单向门'决策摆在我桌上，也许每年我才坐下来，把那扇单向门打开或关上，而这一下就把所有人解放了，我们立刻快了好多。我觉得大家得比以前更快去做那些决策、走过那些门。这点很新、很不一样。我以前是个特别看重'保留选项'的人，但当你能这么快行动、能试那么多东西时，保留选项是要交重税的……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And there's so many reasons this is happening. One is just technology is just every week there's a new shift in what is possible.
turns.zh: 对。而且这事发生的原因太多了。一个就是技术，每个星期'什么可能'都在变。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, if you're spending all these months thinking and planning, just what a waste of time it ends up being because so much is changing.
turns.zh: 所以你要是花好几个月在那想、在那规划，到头来全是浪费时间，因为变化太快了。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I know. Yeah, it's hard to keep up.
turns.zh: 我知道。对，跟不上啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:37:04]. Luckily we got some sweet podcasts to check out, to keep up to date with what's happening. We'll link to yours, of course. (00:37:10): Here's a puzzle for you. What do OpenAI, Cursor, Perplexity, Vercel, Plat, and hundreds of other winning companies have in common? The answer is they're all powered by today's sponsor, WorkOS. If you're building software for enterprises, you've probably felt the pain of integrating single sign-on, SCIM, RBAC, audited logs, and other features required by big customers. WorkOS turns those deal blockers into drop-in APIs, with a modern developer platform built specifically for B2B SaaS. Whether you're a seed-stage startup trying to land your first enterprise customer, or a unicorn expanding globally, WorkOS is the fastest path to becoming enterprise-ready and unlocking growth. (00:37:49): They're essentially Stripe for enterprise features. Visit WorkOS.com to get started, or just hit up their Slack support, where they have real engineers in there who answer your questions super fast. Workos allows you to build like the best, with delightful APIs, comprehensive docs, and a smooth developer experience. Go to WorkOS.com to make your app enterprise-ready today. (00:38:10): Let's talk Halliganisms. Essentially these are nuggets of wisdom and advice that you find yourself sharing often, you've written about a bunch of these online, and so let me just go through them and then just share the synopsis of the advice and the lesson around this Halliganism. The first is, "When you have to eat a shit sandwich, don't nibble."
turns.zh: （听不清00:37:04）还好我们有几档不错的播客可以追，跟得上潮流。当然会放你的链接。（00:37:10）给你出个谜题：OpenAI、Cursor、Perplexity、Vercel、Plat，还有几百家赢家公司，共同点是什么？答案是他们全由今天的赞助商WorkOS驱动。如果你在给企业建软件，你肯定体会过集成单点登录、SCIM、RBAC、审计日志，还有大客户要求的其他功能的痛苦。WorkOS把这些'成交拦路虎'变成即插即用的API，它是一套专为B2B SaaS打造的现代开发者平台。不管你是想拿下第一个企业客户的种子轮创业公司，还是在全球扩张的独角兽，WorkOS都是让你'具备企业级能力'、解锁增长的最快路径。（00:37:49）他们本质上就是企业功能的Stripe。去WorkOS.com开始，或者直接找他们的Slack支持，里面是真工程师，回答超快。WorkOS让你像最牛的人那样开发——愉悦的API、齐全的文档、顺滑的开发体验。今天就上WorkOS.com，让你的app具备企业级能力。（00:38:10）来聊'霍尔甘语录'。其实就是你老挂在嘴边、也写过的那些智慧金句，我过一遍，把建议和道理的梗概讲一下。第一条：'当你不得不吃屎三明治时，别小口小口啃。'

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Okay. Completely stole this from Ruth Porat, the CFO of Google. I saw her quote somewhere, I'm like, that's it, she's put a perfect thing on it. And I'll give you an example where I think this will play out over the next couple of years. I think within the next couple of years there'll be a real retrenchment in valuations, and some will live up to valuations a lot [inaudible 00:38:54]. Like, if I look at the public markets, they're very tight right now, it's like the anti-bubble. And I look at private valuations, it's like a real bubble. I think there's a reckoning somewhere down the road. And a lot of companies are going to have to do layoffs. A lot. It's never fun, it's usually the worst thing in the history of your life, and the temptation is to do, well, just do a little one now and we'll grow into it, and then they do another one in six months, and then another one. (00:39:20): I think with everything, including this type of thing, it's just rip the darn Band-Aid off, tell everyone the bad news, they're adults, they can handle it, and get it done. And I think people avoid that. I think that's good advice Ruth Porat is giving. Because you're going to have bad news to deliver, bad shit is going to happen to your company, even though it looks like it's going amazing right now, weird stuff's going to happen. And you're going to have to deal with it. And we had a lot of weird stuff happen at HubSpot. There's a basketball coach named Mike Krzyzewski, he's Duke's basketball coach. All time winningest college basketball coach ever. If you go to a Duke basketball game, you can hear him yelling from the sidelines, "Let's play, let's play." (00:40:13): And what's going on there is when a college basketball player is playing in the game and takes a shot and clanks it off the rim and misses it, they have a strong tendency to go play overly aggressively on defense in the back court, and many times compound their error by making a foul or something like that. And what he wants to do is people to make their error, forget about it, and move back down the other side of the court and run the play. And so, actually there were times in HubSpot's history where we had the Mike Krzyzewski's face on a huge slide in front of the company meeting, saying, "Next play," because there was an unforced error, and we need to deal with it and move on.
turns.zh: 好。这完全是偷的，从Google的CFO Ruth Porat那。我在哪看到她这句话，当时就想：就它了，她把这事说绝了。我给你举个未来几年会应验的例子。我觉得接下来几年，估值会有一波真正的回撤，有些会配得上它们的估值，有些则……（听不清00:38:54）你看公开市场现在收得很紧，简直是反泡沫；而一级市场估值，像个真泡沫。我觉得迟早有场清算。很多公司得裁员，大裁。这从来不好玩，通常是你人生中最糟的事，而人的诱惑是：先裁一点点，说我们会长回来的，然后六个月又裁一次，再裁一次。（00:39:20）我觉得对任何事——包括这种事——就是咔嚓把创可贴扯下来，把坏消息告诉大家，他们是成年人，扛得住，一次性搞定。我觉得大家都在逃避这个。这是Ruth Porat给的好建议。因为坏消息总会来的，屎一样的事会砸到你公司头上，哪怕现在看着风光无限，怪事就是会发生。你得去面对。HubSpot就出过好多怪事。有个篮球教练叫Mike Krzyzewski，杜克大学的，史上胜场最多的大学篮球教练。你看杜克的比赛，能听见他在场边喊'继续打，继续打'。（00:40:13）那是在说：当一个大学球员投了个三分、哐当砸框没进，他很容易在回防时过度拼命，经常一犯规反而错上加错。而他在……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story of that that comes to mind that is interesting and worth getting into?
turns.zh: 有没有什么具体的故事，既有趣、又值得展开讲讲的？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: There was a lot of them. But I remember in 2000, it was the last day of March in 2019, and we had a really bad outage all day. And we never really had one of those, and it was bad. Customers were unhappy, a lot of customers canceled. I had a lot of customers yelling at me. And I remember that company meeting, I cried in front of the whole company, they couldn't believe it happened to us. And I remember using the Next Play slide on that one. Yeah, we made a lot of mistakes at HubSpot, a lot of bad things happen to companies, and most of them are self-inflicted. And a lot of them are the old saw-like, companies are far more likely to die of overeating than indigestion. Usually it was when we were trying to do too much.
turns.zh: 这种事很多。我记得2019年3月的最后一天，我们一整天都在经历严重的宕机。我们以前从没这样过，那次很惨。客户不爽，好多客户取消了，一堆客户冲我吼。那次全员大会上，我在全公司面前哭了，他们都不敢相信这能发生在我们身上。我记得那次用了'下一球'（Next Play）那页slide。对，HubSpot我们犯过好多错，公司会出好多坏事，而且大多是自己作的。很多都印证了那句老话——公司死于吃撑的概率远大于死于消化不良。通常都是我们想干太多的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I haven't heard that version, I've always heard most companies die have suicide versus homicide. Though indigestion-
turns.zh: 这个说法我没听过，我听过的一直是：大多数公司死于自杀而非他杀。不过消化不良——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: That's true too, by the way.
turns.zh: 那句也对，顺便说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Okay, so next Halliganism, "Never waste a good crisis." That's something that people hear, I'm curious just what's the lesson here, and then is there an example of this where you learned this lesson?
turns.zh: 天哪。好，下一条霍尔甘语录：'永远别浪费一场好危机。'大家常听到这句，我好奇这里的道理是什么，有没有你学到这课的例子？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I'll just follow on to, most of the good things that happened in HubSpot came out of a crisis because we would take pretty drastic measures to fix it and make sure we didn't do the same thing again. And so, in this particular case, we really rethought how we deployed software, how we thought about making software in a way that was incredibly healthy. And we haven't had a serious outage since. The quality is much better. And kind of an interesting thing with HubSpot is we started as a marketing software company, and we pivoted, had Salesforce came into our market, we pivoted into CRM. And one thing that... If your marketing software goes down, if your workflow, if there's a bug in the workflows or something like that, it's bad, but you survive it, you wait a little bit. (00:43:06): If your CRM goes down, particularly on the last day of the quarter, you're really impacting your customer's ability to do business. So, that was a mindset shift that we hadn't quite come to terms with of how important we were to our customers. And so, we made a lot of changes based on that crisis. Usually very good things came out of crises.
turns.zh: 我就顺着说，HubSpot发生的好事，大多是从危机里长出来的，因为我们会采取相当激进的措施去修、确保不再犯。拿这次来说，我们彻底重新想了软件怎么部署、怎么以一种特别健康的方式做软件，从那以后就没再严重宕机过，质量也好了很多。HubSpot还有个有趣的点：我们起步是营销软件公司，后来Salesforce杀进我们市场，我们转去做CRM。有件事……如果你的营销软件挂了，工作流、或者工作流里有个bug，是糟，但你扛得过去，等一会儿就好。（00:43:06）但你的CRM要是挂了，尤其季度最后一天，那真是在影响客户做生意。所以那是一次心智转变——我们还没完全接受'我们对客户有多重要'。于是我们基于那场危机改了好多。通常危机里都长出好东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, there's the lesson there, something's going wrong, is it just like over-correct? Use this as a way to-
turns.zh: 所以那的道理是：出事了，是不是就过度修正、把这当成一个机会去——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. We always over-corrected. Yeah, we almost, we purposely swung the pendulum hard the other way.
turns.zh: 对。我们永远过度修正。对，我们几乎是故意把钟摆狠狠甩到另一边。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which connects to the first Halliganism of, "If you're eating a shit sandwich, don't nibble." It's almost like go all the way, go even further.
turns.zh: 这就连上了第一条霍尔甘语录——'吃屎三明治就别小口啃'，几乎就是：一步到位，甚至走更远。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. Make it really obvious to everyone what's going on.
turns.zh: 对。让所有人都清清楚楚看到发生了什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, another Halliganism, "If you want to kill a plant, have two people water it."
turns.zh: 好，另一条霍尔甘语录：'想养死一盆植物，就找两个人一起浇。'

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I love this one, it's very true. Let's say, Lenny, you bought a new beautiful plant for your office, and then you went away for a month to Turks and Caicos because your AI agent's doing your podcast, and you asked two of your friends, "Hey, would you mind watering my plant?" And there's one of two outcomes what happens to the plant. The plant would either be over-watered and die, or not watered at all and die. And every CEO in the adults' table has gone through this, and they are religious about the DRI. Everyone talks about DRI in the kids' table, but once it gets to the adults' table, people get deep religion on it. (00:44:32): And I think it makes sense. When you're small, and you're in startup mode, everyone's in the room, everyone knows exactly what's going on. So, let's say you're running a pilot project with a big account. You're running that pilot project, everyone's on the same page, the sales person, the service person, developer, everyone's on the same page, and you go out and do it and you execute well. When you get it scale, you've get a sales organization, you've get your [inaudible 00:44:56] deployed engineer organization, you've got your product management organization, you've got some developers working on it. (00:45:00): Everyone's kind of separate, no one knows really what's going on in the other departments. And so, let's say you want to really have a good pilot process, you want to rethink it because you're scaling. Everything important happens cross-functionally inside a company at scale, and you need someone powerful to own it. So, let's say it's a sales person, they need the power to tell people in other divisions what to do, even if they don't own it. So, almost every CEO I deal with is like a zealot on the DRI idea, and it doesn't bite you until you get to some sort of scale.
turns.zh: 我太爱这条了，太对。假设Lenny你给办公室买了盆漂亮的新植物，然后你去Turks and Caicos度一个月假，因为你的AI agent在替你做播客，你托两个朋友：'嘿，帮我浇下花行不？'结果只有两种：要么浇太多淹死，要么根本没人浇干死。大人桌的每个CEO都经历过这个，他们对DRI（直接责任人）这件事信得不行。小孩桌人人都在聊DRI，但一到大人桌，大家就真把它当宗教了。（00:44:32）我觉得这有道理。你小的时候、创业模式里，所有人都在一个屋里，大家都清楚在发生什么。比如你跟一个大客户跑试点项目，销售、服务、开发，所有人一条心，出去执行得很好。等你到规模了，你有销售组织、有现场部署工程师组织、有产品管理组织、有开发在上面做。大家都分开了，没人真知道别的部门在干嘛。所以你想把试点流程搞好、因为要规模化而重做它——规模上来后，重要的事全都是跨部门的，你需要一个有权的人来own它。比如是个销售，他得有权力指挥别的部门的人干啥，哪怕那些人不归他管。所以几乎我接触的每个CEO，都跟DRI这概念成了狂热分子，而且不到一定规模它不咬你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To be super clear about that advice here, it's one person is responsible for a goal, a metric, some outcome you want, versus it may feel like, okay, we have two people on this, it'll be awesome, they'll work together.
turns.zh: 把这建议说透一点：就是一个人对某个目标、某个指标、某个你想要的结果负责，而不是感觉'哦我们派两个人，肯定棒，他们一起干'。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your advice here is that doesn't work?
turns.zh: 你的建议是那样不行？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Communities never work. Yes.
turns.zh: 委员会从来不行。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. And DRI is directly responsible individual.
turns.zh: 对。而DRI是直接责任人（directly responsible individual）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I always thought about this is just having someone's ass on the line for something makes them so motivated to get it done, versus spreading the responsibility and the upside and the downside, it just doesn't work.
turns.zh: 我一贯的想法是：让某个人为某事'后背着火'，他才有动力去搞定；而不是把责任、收益、风险摊给两个人，那样就是不行。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I totally agree with you.
turns.zh: 我完全同意你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, another Halliganism, I don't know if you put it this way, the way I think about it is this idea of, "There's no such thing as a silver bullet, it just takes a lot of lead bullets to get something done." I think the way you wrote about it is it's always one step forward, two steps back. Talk about your advice there.
turns.zh: 好。另一条霍尔甘语录，不知道你是不是这么表述的，我是这么理解的：'世上没有银弹，要把事做成，得靠一堆铅弹。'我觉得你写的是'永远进一步、退两步'。聊聊你这条。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yeah, I always thought, incorrectly, that we would have one hire or one investor or one event or one product release that would... I was wrong about this, but it'd be a silver bullet. And the reality inside the HubSpot machine, the way it felt to me, it looks from the outside, over a long time up into the right, and smooth, but inside it was two steps forward, one step back, two steps forward, one step back, two steps forward, one step back. And a lot of times it was a crisis that caused that step back. So, we just didn't have that. (00:47:02): The thing about being a founder/CEO is no one, especially when you're in your 20s, there's no one there to rescue you. Your parents aren't going to rescue you, your VC is not going to rescue you, your teacher, your thesis advisor, you're on your own and you got to figure it out. And that hits you when you hit your first crisis, it's on you. You can get some help, but it's on you.
turns.zh: 对，我以前一直错误地以为，我们会靠一次招聘、一个投资人、一个事件、一次产品发布就……我以为那是银弹，我错了。但HubSpot这台机器里的真实感受是：外面看是长期向右上、平滑上升，里面其实是进两步、退一步，进两步、退一步。而且很多时候，是危机造成了那次后退。所以我们就是没有银弹。（00:47:02）当创始人兼CEO最残酷的是——没人，尤其你二十来岁时，没人来救你。父母不会，投资人不会，老师、论文导师都不会，你只能自己扛、自己想办法。这感觉在你撞上第一次危机时击中你——是你的事。你能拿到点帮助，但终究是你的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes they have you in their corner, if they're lucky at Sequoia. Plug, plug.
turns.zh: 运气好的话，他们在红杉那边还有你撑腰。插播一下，插播一下。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yep. I can't solve it oftentimes, I can be the shoulder they cry on, and I can give them advice, but it's still on them.
turns.zh: 对。我也常常解不了，我可以是他们哭诉的肩膀、可以给建议，但终究是他们的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like too many people start companies just like... When someone comes to you like, hey Brian, should I start a company? I have this idea. Do you often just like, no. You have no idea what you're getting into, this is going to be much more painful?
turns.zh: 你会不会觉得太多人随随便便就开公司——有人来找你说'嘿Brian，我要不要开个公司？我有个点子。'你是不是经常直接说'不，你根本不知道你要跳进什么火坑，这会痛苦得多'？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. Yes. I heard Jensen Huang say that. "I wouldn't have start started Nvidia if I had it to do over." If someone asked me that question, I would start HubSpot over. It was very hard, there were a lot of sacrifices, it wasn't glamorous at all. But in the end of the day, I'm incredibly proud of it. And on my deathbed, I can look back and really enjoy it. And the Dalai Lama's got a good expression like, "Live a good life so you can live it again on your deathbed." And I'm really glad I did it. But I do talk a lot of founders out of it. The obsession is real, you have to be deeply obsessed. And all these founders and CEOs I talk to, people talk about 9-9-6, it's way more than that. The founders are seven days a week, they're always on, I [inaudible 00:48:40] on Sunday nights, it's full contact. (00:48:43): And I think what's going on there, particularly now, is people just see this massive platform change, massive opportunity, they don't want to waste the opportunity. So, I think that mindset's right. But people today are much, much more hardcore than they were in my year. I worked hard, and I was probably, I was 60 to 70 week hours a week the entire time, never really turned it off. But that's kind of how I thought about it. It's different now. People are much more focused, and I think Elon's inspired people.
turns.zh: 对，对。我听Jensen Huang说过：'要是重来一次，我不会开Nvidia。'如果有人问我这问题，我会选择再开一次HubSpot。它非常难，牺牲很多，一点都不光鲜。但到头来，我骄傲得不行。临死前我能回头，真的享受它。达赖喇嘛有句话挺好：'好好活，这样你临终前能再活一遍。'我很高兴我干了。但我确实劝退过很多创始人。那种痴迷是真的，你必须深度痴迷。而我聊的这些创始人、CEO，大家说996，其实远不止。创始人是连轴转七天，时刻在线，我（听不清00:48:40）周日晚上也绷着，全程贴身肉搏。（00:48:43）我觉得尤其现在，是人们看到了巨大的平台变化、巨大的机会，不想浪费。所以这种心态是对的。但今天的人比我那会儿狠得多。我干得也狠，大概一周六十到七十小时、全程不断电。但那是我的活法。现在不一样，人更专注，我觉得是Elon启发了大家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had a start back in the day, nowhere near as successful as HubSpot, but the way I thought about it is, let me just give it everything I have and see what I can do. This is the shot, this is my chance, let me just give it all. Forget balance, just go for it. Seven days a week for a while. And then you scale back. And it's just such an empowering thing to do for a while, just like, let me just try. This won't be forever.
turns.zh: 我当年也创过业，远没HubSpot成功，但我的想法是：就把我的一切都押上，看我能干成啥。这是机会，是我的 shot，全压上，忘了平衡，去干。连轴转一阵子，然后再收。这种'豁出去干一阵'特别给人力量，就觉得：让我试试，又不会是一辈子。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I know you've written about this, just like balance for CEO is not, you should not have work-life balance if you want to be incredibly successful. I don't know if that's always true, but just... I don't know, how do you talk about that to founders?
turns.zh: 我知道你写过这个——对CEO来说平衡是不存在的，想极其成功就别想着工作生活平衡。我不确定这是不是永远对，但……你怎么跟创始人聊这个？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: I don't know any of the founders I work with that have work-life balance. By the way, this is not something I recommend. I didn't have it, I don't think my co-founder, Dharmesh had it. The only CEO I know, and he's unusual in this way, is Kareem from Clay. He's like, "Nope, you need balance, take the weekends..." He's got a different mindset. I'm going to have him on my pod to talk about his mindset. But he's sort of the outlier, everyone else is really, really obsessed, and they really don't have much of a life.
turns.zh: 我认识的创始人里，没有一个有工作生活平衡。顺便说，这我不推荐。我没有，我联合创始人Dharmesh也没有。唯一一个、而且他在这方面很反常的，是Clay的Kareem。他说：'不，你得有平衡，周末……'他想法不一样。我会请他上我的播客聊他的心态。但他算是异类，其他人都真·痴迷，基本没生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It did take them a long time to find product market fit [inaudible 00:50:25]-
turns.zh: 他们找到产品市场契合花了挺久（听不清00:50:25）——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: [inaudible 00:50:25] definitely pre-AI. It did them a long...
turns.zh: （听不清00:50:25）肯定是AI之前。他们花了好久……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder if there's a correlation, but it did work out.
turns.zh: 我在想有没有相关性，但反正成了。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Worked out great.
turns.zh: 成得特别好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it is a good lesson. Okay, a few more here. One is, it's a math formula. "EV is greater than TV is greater than MEV." What is that?
turns.zh: 所以这是个好教训。好，再来几条。一个是数学公式：'EV大于TV大于MEV'。这是什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Okay, EV is enterprise value, TV is your team's value, MEV is your value. And as HubSpot was scaling, and we had a lot of people who were VPs in different roles, and they started to get good-sized organizations, where they would fall down was they didn't solve for MEV, but they'd solve for TV over EV. They'd solve for their own team. So, let's say they ran sales, and say, I just want bookings to be as high as possible because I get paid on bookings, and the service team can handle all the downstream problems I created. Marketing to sales... Between every department that's happened. And the kind of immature managers who didn't scale, really solved for themselves, and as they solved for themselves kind of sub-optimize for their peers. And their employees would notice it and complain about it, it would be fine in the short term, but it would show up. (00:51:44): And the place it would show up, Lenny, was, we did, and I think a lot of companies do this now, but we did a quarterly employee net promoter. We did a quarterly customer net promoter survey and a quarterly employee one. And we would have people rate it by the department they're in. And one interesting thing about that, so it's like sales and service and engineering, all the different departments, and we had an overall net promoter score, and then each department had a net promoter score. And let's just take sales. Sales net promoter score was like, 65, 62, 68, 30. Ooh, that's a big drop. And then you read the comments and it was not good, a lot of complaints about the leader of that. And a lot of the complaints were a little bit of this TV thing. (00:52:34): And then, we give feedback to that VP, would help them, we give them all the comments, be like, you got this. And then a quarter later from 30 to -5. And they almost never actually recovered. When you lose, your team can't... It's hard to get them back. And that's why I say hire slow, fire fast. And this doesn't show up in the first 100, 150 employees, everyone's solving for EV, but as it gets bigger, and the CEO doesn't know anyone, and there's a couple layers between you and the employees, they tend to solve for TV. So, we always put on the wall, "Solve for EV over TV over MEV," and then we added CV in front of EV, solve for the customers first, then for HubSpot, then the employee, then yourself. That was be very helpful to us.
turns.zh: EV是企业价值（enterprise value），TV是你团队的价值，MEV是你自己的价值。HubSpot在规模化时，很多不同岗位的VP手上都有不小的团队，他们栽跟头的地方是：他们不为MEV解，却为了TV压过EV——他们只为自己的团队解。比如他管销售，就想'我的bookings越高越好，因为我拿bookings提成，后面的烂摊子服务团队去收拾'。营销对销售……部门之间全是这种事。那些没 scale 起来的不成熟管理者，真就是为自己解，为自己解的时候就把同辈给次优化了。他们的下属会注意到、会抱怨，短期没事，但总会暴露。（00:51:44）暴露的地方Lenny，是我们——我觉得很多公司现在都做——做了个季度员工净推荐值。我们做了季度的客户净推荐调查和季度的员工版。我们让人按所在部门打分。有意思的是：销售、服务、工程，所有部门，有个总净推荐分，每个部门也有一个。拿销售来说，销售净推荐分是65、62、68、30。哦，大跌。然后你看评论，不好看，一堆对这个领导的抱怨，很多就是这种TV心态。（00:52:34）然后我们给那个VP反馈、把评论全给他、说'你这有点问题'。结果下一个季度从30掉到负5。而且他们几乎从来没有真正恢复过来。你一旦失去团队，就……很难拉回来。所以我才说招人慢、开人快。而这在一百、一百五十人之前不会显出来……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I imagine everybody listening, working at a big company understands this. Where you have goals, you get your KPIs, and your performance reviews based on what impact you drive, if you hit your goals. And so, the incentives are focused on my goals and drive those, and I don't care about other people's goals, the company's goals-
turns.zh: 对，我猜每个在大公司干活、听这期的人都能理解。你有目标、有KPI、绩效评估看的是你驱动的影响，只要你达标。所以激励全盯着我自己的目标，我不管别人的目标、公司的目标——

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Steve Jobs had an interesting line, he says, "You don't work for your boss, you work for Apple." I thought that was pretty good. And I heard that after I was CEO of HubSpot, but that kind of captures the sentiment. And that's how I felt about HubSpot. You work for HubSpot first and then you work for your boss.
turns.zh: Steve Jobs有句有意思的话：'你不是为你老板干活，你为苹果干活。'我觉得挺好。我是当完HubSpot CEO才听到这句的，但它把那感觉说中了。我对HubSpot就是这感觉：你先为HubSpot干，再为你老板干。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is hard because people's performance reviews are based on their goals, KPIs, it's always like, here's what I got to drive. Other than putting posters on the wall, and this is our, just HubSpot growth above all is what matters, or our customers, I guess in your case. Is there anything tactically that was useful in helping people prioritize enterprise value?
turns.zh: 这很难，因为人的绩效评估是基于自己的目标、KPI，永远是'这是我要驱动的'。除了在墙上贴海报——'HubSpot增长高于一切'、或者'客户高于一切'——你这边还有什么实操办法，能帮人把企业价值排前面？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: This was explicitly called out in the form for the employee when you got your review, this was part of it. And so, they get a score of one to, I forget, 10 on that. I would talk about it constantly. And when we first started HubSpot, I ran it a little bit like Jensen runs NVIDIA, where I didn't do one-on-ones, and I gave a lot of good and bad feedback publicly in large management team meetings, and I definitely would go out of my way to criticize people if I felt like they were solving for TV over EV. And people got a sense for that. And then, every quarter we did a really well-produced company meeting, we spent a lot of time on it, and at the end of the company meeting, we gave out, we called them the Champaigner Awards, it was a bottle of Veuve, that my co-founder and I signed. And we'd read something nice about them and give it to them, and usually there was an EV team in that. And so, we did different things to kind of beat that into people's heads.
turns.zh: 这在我们给员工的评估表上被明确写出来了，是其中一项。所以他们会在这项上打个分，一到十我忘了。我会不停地讲这事。HubSpot刚开时，我有点像Jensen管Nvidia那样——我不做一对一，在大管理会上公开给大量好和坏的反馈，而且如果我觉得有人在TV压EV，我绝对会专门去批。大家就感应到了。然后每个季度我们搞一场制作精良的全员大会，花很多时间，结束时发奖，我们叫'香槟奖'（Champaigner Awards），一瓶我和我联合创始人签名的Veuve。我们会念一段关于他们的好话、把酒给他们，通常里头都有个EV团队。所以我们用了各种办法把这事砸进人脑子里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So, here is just celebrate people that focus on this, and also included in their valuation performance reviews.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以就是：表彰那些盯企业价值的人，而且把它写进他们的绩效评估里。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That's a good segue to another Halliganism where you talk about how companies are either customer-centric or investor-centric, and it's really important to know which you are. And you guys actually shifted there. What's your insight there?
turns.zh: 好。这自然过渡到另一条霍尔甘语录：你说公司要么是客户中心、要么是投资人中心，搞清楚自己是哪种特别重要。而且你们当时还真转变了。你有什么洞见？

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Okay. We were very employee-centric, more than customer-centric in the first several years of HubSpot. So much so that the company was number one on Glassdoor's best place to work, I was the number one CEO on Glassdoor, and as I look back at that, I'm not sure that's a good thing. Wanting to be liked I don't think is a good feature of a CEO, and wanting to be the best place to work probably isn't the right way to go. If you look at Toby from Shopify, his scores aren't that good, but that company is doing really, really well. And so, we over-indexed on it, and part of the reason we over-indexed on it is my co-founder was really strong in this, and we had an incredibly powerful head of HR, named Katie Burke, and we just worked on it. We spent a lot of time on it. And when we'd have a management team meeting, and let's say it's four hours long, two of the four hours would be on employee stuff. (00:56:28): And at some point I was like, why are we spending so much time on employee net promoter scores? Let's say our employee net promoter score was 60, and our customer net promoter score is 25, I was like, we need to take... I would give up 10 points of employee net promoter score to get 10 points of customer net promoter score. And so, over some time we shifted the center of gravity to customers, and we still of course, worried about employees, but the center of gravity from HubSpot moves very much to customers. And we did that in a few ways. Every time we had a management team meeting... We had our management team meetings once a month, not once a week, and we would have a customer panel come on, and that customer panel, I would run the panel, and ask very tricky questions to the customers, and pull out the bad news from that. (00:57:22): And then, we still do this, we have a customer panel at our board meetings. Our whole board can ask questions. And my favorite question is, what do you love about HubSpot? And then... And then, what do you hate about HubSpot? And they kind of look at their shoes. And you're like, come on. And it's a great way... So, the employee's voice is here, those company meetings, we have the customers at the company meetings. We changed the comp plan, so the management team got paid not on revenue but on retention and net promoter score. And so we worked very hard and swung the pendulum to customer-centric. But I do think companies have one center of gravity or another.
turns.zh: 好。HubSpot头几年，我们是员工中心，胜过客户中心。夸张到公司在Glassdoor'最佳雇主'排第一，我是Glassdoor上排第一的CEO。现在回头看，我不觉得那是好事。'想被喜欢'我觉得不是CEO的好特质，想当'最佳雇主'大概也不是对的路子。你看Shopify的Toby，他分数不咋地，但那公司牛得不行。所以我们过度往这头偏了，部分原因是我联合创始人在这块特别强，我们还有个极强的HR负责人Katie Burke，我们就一直在这上花时间。管理会要是开四小时，其中两小时都在聊员工的事。（00:56:28）有天我就想：咱干嘛花这么多时间在员工净推荐分上？假设员工净推荐分是60，客户净推荐分是25，我是想：我宁愿拿10分员工净推荐分，去换10分客户净推荐分。于是过了一段时间，我们把重心挪到了客户。当然员工我们还在乎，但HubSpot的重心非常明显地移向了客户。我们用了几招。每次管理会——我们一个月一次，不是一周一次——我们会请一组客户来，我主持，问他们很刁钻的问题，把坏消息挖出来。（00:57:22）而且我们到现在还这么做，董事会上也放客户panel，整个董事会都能问。我最喜欢的问题是：你最爱HubSpot什么？然后……然后，你最恨HubSpot什么？他们……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a really interesting thread throughout this conversation of just, when do you want to change how you operate you have to go really far to a whole other... And to almost over-correct to... Yeah, it's a really interesting of just how much work it takes to change culture, to change your norms.
turns.zh: 这整期聊下来有个很有意思的线：当你要改变自己的运作方式，你得走得很远、走到另一个极端，几乎过度修正才能……对，改变文化、改变习惯，要花多大功夫，这真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes. And the bigger it is, the more obvious you have to make it. And the other thing about being a CEO, Lenny, is you got to say the same thing over and over and over and over and over again. It just doesn't sink into people's heads, you have to just be incredibly repetitive on it before it sinks in. Same thing with marketing, but internally, and that happens. The other weird thing about being a CEO, Lenny, is as it gets bigger... When it's small, everyone's giving you shit, and you're all on the same level. But as it gets bigger, you didn't interview everyone, you have thousands of employees, you don't know everyone, and people put you on a pedestal that you don't deserve. (00:58:53): And let's say you're in the hallway, and you're just kind of shooting the shit with a bunch of people, and you're like, ah, it'd be cool if we had a product that did... Somebody inevitably would go home and build that thing, and be like, Brian wants this as a big initiative. So, people really lock in on what you said. And it turns out you have to be very repetitive and you have to be very careful what you say.
turns.zh: 对。而且越大，你就得做得越明显。当CEO还有件怪事Lenny：同一句话你得翻来覆去、翻来覆去、翻来覆去地说。它根本渗不进人的脑子，你得重复到极致它才沉下去。营销也一样，但内部更甚。还有件怪事：公司越大……小的时候，人人都怼你，大家一个level。但大了，你没面试过所有人，几千号员工你不认识，人就把你供到一个你配不上的台子上。（00:58:53）比如你在走廊，跟一帮人瞎聊，随口说'要是有个能做……的产品就酷了'，保不准谁回家就把那玩意做出来，然后说'Brian要把这个当大项目'。所以人真的会死锁在你说的话上。结果就是你得极度重复，而且得极度小心你说了什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Dharmesh was on the podcast, your illustrious co-founder, and he developed a whole system to avoid this sort of thing. Flash tags, where it's like, this is just an FYI.
turns.zh: Dharmesh上过这播客，你那位牛气的联合创始人，他搞了整套系统来避开这种事——flash tags，比如'这只是一句FYI'。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: We had a whole system. Because we would say something on an email to the management team, or Slack, and everyone would be like, okay, this is what they want, let's do it. And sometimes it is like, you need to do this, and sometimes it is like, we should talk about doing this, and sometimes it is, this is just kind of an FYI, we're thinking about it. And because it got big, we came up with that rubric of, we needed to tag each email with, do you want me to get this done this week, or is this something we should talk about, or is this something that's just FYI, I'm thinking about?
turns.zh: 我们有一整套。因为我们在邮件或Slack上对管理团队说句啥，人人都'哦，这是他们要的，干'。有时是'你得干这个'，有时是'我们应该聊聊这个'，有时是'我就是随口一想、FYI'。因为大了，我们搞出那个规矩：每封邮件都得打标签——你是想我这周就搞定，还是想我们聊聊，还是只是FYI、我在想这事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that... One of them is plea. Pleading you to do it. I'm not telling you to do this, I'm just pleading that you do what I ask. Oh man. Okay. This all connects. And by the way, you guys were co-founders for 20 years, you shared something before we started recording. So, Dharmesh famously did not ever want direct reports, he's just like, Brian, I want to start this with you, but I don't want to ever manage anyone. And you were talking about how you had to take on engineering, which didn't make any sense.
turns.zh: 我喜欢……其中一个是plea（恳求）。恳求你去做。我不是命令你，只是恳求你按我说的做。天哪。好，这些都连上了。顺便，你们俩做了二十年联合创始人，录音前你分享了件事。Dharmesh出了名地从不想要直接下属，他就说'Brian，我想跟你开这公司，但我永远不想管任何人'。而你说过你被迫接了工程，这本来毫无道理。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: No, I'm an engineer and I can code, but it's not good. So, when we started the company he's like, "I was a CEO before, I was terrible at it, I don't want to do it again, you're going to be the CEO." I'm like, "Great." And he's like, "And by the way, I'm not going to have any direct reports." I'm like, "Well, it's just the two of us so don't have worry about it." He's like, "No, ever, never." I'm like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah." And then we get 10, 12 people, we're starting to hire engineers, and onboard them, and making up big decisions, and I would go to him and be like, "Well, can you manage him?" He is like, "Don't you remember I told you I don't want to have any direct reports?" It's like, "Surely you were kidding when you said that?" He said, "Nope." And so, Dharmesh Shah has never had a single direct report at HubSpot.
turns.zh: 对，我会写代码，但不咋地。刚开公司时他说：'我以前当过CEO，糟透了，不想再干，你来当CEO。'我说'好啊'。他说'顺便，我不会有任何直接下属。'我说'现在就咱俩，不用担心'。他说'不，永远，绝不。'我说'行行行'。然后我们到十个人、十二个人，开始招工程师、做onboard、做重大决策，我去找他说'那你能管他吗？'他说'你忘了我说过不要直接下属？'我说'你那会儿肯定是开玩笑吧？'他说'没。'所以Dharmesh Shah在HubSpot从来没有任何直接下属。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible. I don't, it's just like a dream, a way to operate, I love that you made it possible for him, and it created all this opportunity for him to tinker and innovate.
turns.zh: 不可思议。我就觉得，这是一种梦幻的运作方式，我喜欢你让他能这样，这给他创造了大量去鼓捣、去创新的空间。

turns.speaker: Brian Halligan
turns.en: Yes, yes, it freed him up to really think and be creative.
turns.zh: 对，对，这把他解放出来真正去想、去创造。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I'm excited to get him back on the podcast someday, we're going to link to that episode. Maybe a last question, I'm curious if there's anything else you think we missed?
